title: On Graph Grammars and Games
text:
Puzzle games form a fascinating class of 2D games due to their challenging and entertaining nature. However the creation of these games traditionally required immense manpower and time, thereby escalating the cost of developing these games. In order to avoid boredom on the part of players a game developer needs to provide new domains to the player so that the game becomes unpredictable. Making use of algorithms for creating these environments helps developers to produce new challenges at a lower cost. In this paper we look at certain categories of 2D games - specifically games having lock-and-key [1] patterns as challenges.

Any system where items are interconnected in some way, such as a network of computers, a city and its roads [2], or a group of friends on a social network, aquatic predatory networks, plant pollinator networks, etc. can be represented using graphs. As the game design methodology used here is algorithmic in nature, the best data structure that complements this approach is a graph. In this paper we employ graph grammars as a mechanism for creating these game plots/levels. We have designed an algorithm which randomly generates a new game plot each time the game is played, ensuring a stimulating experience for the players.

The rest of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 presents the key concepts associated with game design and graph grammars required for understanding the rest of this paper. Sections 3 and 4 develop a modified version of the nc-eNCE and jumping graph grammars introduced in [3,4] so as to deal with directed graphs. Finally Section 5 deals with two dimensional game generation and shows how the modified graph grammars discussed in Sections 3 and 4 can be used to generate solvable game plots. It also includes an algorithm for generating these plots randomly.
